summary: This memo is a report on a Gateway Special Interest Group meeting held at ISI on 28 and 29 February 1984, with about 35 gateway designers and implementers. It is based on notes by Jon Postel and Mike Muuss, organized by topic. It records discussion, not a protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: These are notes from a meeting of people who build routers. They wrote down what was said, topic by topic, so others who missed it can catch up.

subtitle: Notes from a 1984 meeting of Internet gateway designers on routing and network interconnection.

tldr.problem: Gateway designers and Internet routing researchers gathered in February 1984 to share designs, implementations, and ideas as the network expanded and the routing infrastructure needed to scale.
tldr.mechanism: About 35 engineers from MIT, BBN, CMU, SRI, Lincoln Labs, MITRE and other institutions presented their gateway and router designs, their experience with the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP), and emerging ideas about routing algorithms, address translation, and congestion control.
tldr.outcome: The meeting documented a snapshot of early 1980s gateway technology: diverse hardware (PDP-11s, MC68000s, specialized processors), varied routing strategies (EGP, SPF, stub gateways, multi-processor architectures), and emerging challenges like scaling GGP routing tables, handling congestion, and interconnecting networks with different technologies.

today: RFC 898 is a historic document capturing the state of Internet gateway technology in early 1984. The meeting addressed problems that would be solved in subsequent years: GGP was replaced by OSPF, EGP evolved into BGP (Border Gateway Protocol), and the Internet grew to handle millions of hosts and billions of packets. Many of the challenges discussed—congestion control, multi-path routing, quality of service, mobile networks—remain relevant today.

sections.title: The Gateway Special Interest Group Meeting
sections.content:
RFC 898 is a report on the Gateway Special Interest Group meeting held on February 28 and 29, 1984, at ISI in Marina del Rey, California. Robert Hinden of BBN chaired the meeting, and Jon Postel of ISI hosted it. About 35 gateway designers and implementors attended from universities, research labs, and commercial vendors. The memo contains notes based on recollections by Jon Postel and Mike Muuss, organized by presentation topic.

This was not a standards-setting meeting and contains no conclusions, decisions, or policy statements. Rather, it is a record of what researchers and implementors were doing with gateway and routing technology in early 1984, and what problems they were trying to solve. The meeting covered both hardware designs (the MIT C gateway, the BBN Butterfly, the CMU and BRL gateways) and software and algorithmic ideas (SPF routing, address mapping, congestion control).
sections.plainLanguage: A group of people who design and build routers met for two days and wrote down what everyone talked about. It's not a rule, just notes on what people were building and thinking about.

sections.title: Gateway Hardware and Software Designs
sections.content:
Presentations on specific gateway implementations revealed diverse hardware approaches. MIT presented a C-language gateway running on 11/03 and 11/23 computers, as well as on 68000 processors, capable of 100 to 180 packets per second. The gateway handled multiple protocols (Internet, DECnet, Chaosnet) and used a three-level routing strategy (GGP for gateway-to-gateway communication, EGP for exterior gateways, IGP for interior gateways).

BBN discussed the Butterfly gateway, a multiprocessor system using MC68000s interconnected by a special switch, designed to replace 30 aging PDP-11 'core' gateways. The Butterfly promised to support thousands of networks and new features like type-of-service routing and flow control. CMU described a simpler dumb gateway in C (derived from MIT's design) running on a host using minimal memory (32K buffers) and a custom operating system. BRL presented a gateway based on the LOS (Logical Operating System) design, which emphasized message passing and memory management without data copying.

Presentations also covered specialized gateways: Lincoln Labs discussed a high-speed gateway for the WBCNET handling packet voice and achieving 900 to 1000 packets per second. MITRE described minimal stub gateways using inexpensive Intel 186 processors. Ford (FACC) presented a distributed multiprocessor architecture with a special 90 megabit-per-second bus and multi-level routing.
sections.plainLanguage: Different labs built routers in different ways: some small and simple, some powerful with multiple processors, some for experiments like sending voice through the network. They compared how many packets per second each could handle.

sections.title: Routing Algorithms and Protocols
sections.content:
A major theme was routing: how gateways decide where to send packets. The meeting discussed the limitations of the existing Gateway-to-Gateway Protocol (GGP), which was used in the ARPANET core. GGP had problems: routing updates could become very large (100+ networks in an update), neighbor probes created excessive traffic (N-squared complexity with N gateways), and buffers were small.

Presentations introduced the Shortest Path First (SPF) algorithm, later used in OSPF (Open Shortest Path First). SPF built a complete topology map and used Dijkstra's algorithm to calculate the shortest path. Unlike GGP, which only tracked reachability, SPF could use delay as a metric and support type-of-service (ToS) routing—choosing different paths based on quality-of-service requirements.

The meeting also discussed multiple-constraint routing, where paths are selected on more than one criterion (e.g., minimum delay with a minimum packet size), and address mapping and translation for interconnecting different network types. The EGP protocol was a continuing topic; presenters discussed its strengths (autonomous system partitioning, decoupling of implementations) and weaknesses (slow update rate, rigid tree-structured topology, incomplete neighbor acquisition).
sections.plainLanguage: People showed how their routers decided which way to send packets. The old way (GGP) was slow and used too much network traffic. The new way (SPF) was smarter: calculate the whole map and find the best path.

sections.title: Congestion, Performance, and Scaling
sections.content:
Congestion and flow control emerged as critical challenges. John Nagle (Ford) presented ideas that would later become RFC 896, arguing that hosts and gateways must not drop packets unnecessarily and that hosts should behave responsibly. He identified problematic TCP implementations (DEC TOPS-20 TCP and 4.2BSD VAX/UNIX) that sent many small packets, causing congestion. His suggested solution: when a TCP sends, initiate a send only if there are no outstanding packets on the connection, and when a gateway nears overload, send ICMP Source Quench messages before dropping packets.

Other presentations covered capacity planning: each node should have at least one buffer per TCP connection plus overload buffers; memory size has limits beyond which more doesn't help. Lincoln Labs reported achieving 900-1000 packets per second with specialized I/O interfaces. Various gateways reported effective bandwidth, jitter, and latency measurements on links ranging from 2.5 Mbps (ARCNET) to 9.6 Kbps leased lines to 1 Mbps Ethernets.

The meeting also touched on emerging problems: interconnecting incompatible networks (X.25, ARCNET, Ethernet, satellite links), address translation and mapping, support for multimedia (voice and data), and mobile hosts. These topics foreshadowed work on network gateways, domain names, and quality-of-service routing.
sections.plainLanguage: People talked about what happens when a router gets too much traffic and how to keep the network from getting clogged. They shared how fast their systems actually ran in real tests.
